newsitem.title: USA: Clinton vows to tighten Saddam's 'strait-jacket'.
newsitem.headline: Clinton vows to tighten Saddam's 'strait-jacket'.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Saturday said the U.S. military had "tightened the strategic strait-jacket" on Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein, one day after ordering additional American troops to the Gulf.

"America's policy has been to contain Saddam, to reduce the threat he poses to the region and to do it in a way that makes him pay a price when he acts recklessly," Clinton said in his weekly radio address.
He said he ordered missile strikes on Iraq last week in order to extend the so-called no-fly zones where Iraqi military planes were banned.
"This action tightened the strategic strait-jacket on Saddam, making it harder for him to threaten Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, and easier for us to stop him if he does," Clinton said.
Before the address was broadcast, Clinton spoke by telephone with Saudi Arabia's King Fahd, even as Defense Secretary William Perry was traveling to the region for meetings with Gulf leaders.

Perry's tour was expected to include stops in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain and Turkey, and was aimed at securing support for possible U.S. attacks and for enforcing the expanded no-fly zones over Iraq.
Saudi Arabia has tried to distance itself from the latest military strikes against Iraq, including last week's missile attacks on Iraqi air defenses.

Clinton said involvement in this latest Gulf crisis advanced "America's fundamental interests in the region," which he said included the fight against terrorism and the preservation of a free flow of oil.

He stressed that U.S. interests also include protection of troops in the region, and vowed to take "whatever steps are necessary" to protect American pilots in the area. "I have ordered sufficient forces to the region to give us that capability," Clinton said.

On Friday, Clinton ordered 5,000 infantry troops to Kuwait to join 1,200 soldiers already holding exercises near the Iraqi border, despite Baghdad's pledge to stop attacking U.S. warplanes patrolling the southern no-fly zone.
The troops, based at Fort Hood, Texas, made final preparations to leave on Saturday. Defense officials at the base said the actual deployment from there would be about 3,000 troops.

White House National Security Adviser Anthony Lake called Baghdad's pledge "welcome," but sounded skeptical in televised comments late on Friday on ABC-TV's "Nightline" program: "We'll have to see what he does on the ground."

Lake said he was confident the United States could prevent another Iraqi invasion of Kuwait, the action that prompted the 1991 Gulf War. "I think we can deter him, and if he were to invade Kuwait, defeat him."
The latest U.S. troops heading for Kuwait were part of a buildup in the Gulf that also includes sending more planes and warships to the region.

Eight radar-dodging Stealth warplanes have already arrived in Kuwait and a second U.S. aircraft carrier, the Enterprise, is steaming toward the Gulf. This would bring the force there to over 150 Navy aircraft and over 20 other warships and submarines, many armed with cruise missiles.
